item.title: Connecting to Access Databases from Java: UCanAccess Setup and Usage
item.description:
“Connecting to Access Databases from Java: UCanAccess Setup and Usage”

Are you developing Java applications that need to interact with Microsoft Access databases (.accdb or .mdb files)? A common challenge is finding a direct JDBC driver for Access. Fortunately, the UCanAccess driver offers a robust, pure Java solution that bypasses the need for ODBC configurations. This driver leverages the Jackcess and HSQLDB libraries to provide seamless read and write access to Access files.

item.title: PDO Query Errors: Get Messages & Fix LIMIT Clause Issues
item.description:
“PDO Query Errors: Get Messages & Fix LIMIT Clause Issues”

Encountering silent query failures with PDO can be a significant roadblock in application development. This post delves into common PDO issues and provides clear, actionable solutions to get your database interactions running smoothly.

How to Retrieve PDO Error Messages When Queries Fail

When your PDO queries aren’t producing the expected results and you’re not seeing any explicit error messages, it’s often due to the error reporting mode not being configured to reveal these issues. The recommended approach is to set PDO’s error mode to exceptions. This method offers several advantages over standard errors: exceptions include a stack trace, can be managed with try...catch blocks, or directed to a dedicated error handler. Even when unhandled, they function like typical PHP errors, adhering to your site’s overall error reporting configuration.

item.title: PostgreSQL Timestamps: Time Zones Explained
item.description:
“PostgreSQL Timestamps: Time Zones Explained”

PostgreSQL offers two distinct timestamp data types: timestamp with time zone (often abbreviated as timestamptz) and timestamp without time zone (abbreviated as timestamp). timestamptz is generally considered the preferred choice for managing date and time information due to its robust time zone handling capabilities.

Internal Storage and Epoch:

Internally, both timestamp types use 8 bytes for storage, representing microseconds from the PostgreSQL epoch, which is January 1, 2000, 00:00:00 UTC. PostgreSQL also natively understands Unix time, which counts seconds from the Unix epoch (January 1, 1970, 00:00:00 UTC). This is utilized in functions like to_timestamp(double precision) and EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM timestamptz).
